title: Entropy seed and warmup playbook for throughput runs
body:
Purpose:
This playbook codifies pragmatic, reproducible warmup and seeding techniques for throughput-oriented benchmarking of the serving runtime. It focuses on minimizing run-to-run variance caused by priming/entropy, ensuring deterministic start states where possible, and capturing the signals we need to explain throughput regressions (token/sec, p99 tails, GPU occupancy).

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to microbenchmark and production-like throughput experiments (not model training).
- Assumes model artifacts are pinned (model hash or container image) and the runtime is configured as it would be for a Dedicated node (no autoscaling during run).
- Hardware topology must be constant across comparative runs (same instance type, same CUDA driver/kernel versions).

Key definitions:
- Priming: any request history or prefix tokens that initialize KV cache and execution state prior to measurement window.
- Entropy seed: RNG seed(s) used by the load generator and any stochastic sampling in the model pipeline.
- Warmup window: the time or number of requests dedicated to bringing caches, batching paths, and kernels into steady-state before the measurement window begins.

High-level goals:
1) Make runs reproducible across engineers and CI.
2) Separate warmup effects from steady-state metrics.
3) Make instrumentation cheap to enable long runs.
4) Capture deterministic traces enabling root-cause analysis when throughput changes.

Load generator configuration guidelines:
- Arrival pattern: prefer Poisson with fixed mean for steady-state runs; use scheduled bursts for microburst tests.
- Concurrency vs QPS: control only one variable at a time. For concurrency-focused tests use fixed-concurrency arrival; for throughput-focused tests drive QPS and let runtime admit.
- Sequence length distribution: model real workload histogram (p10/p50/p90/p99). Provide an explicit distribution file in bench assets.
- Prompt templates: ship a set of 100–500 representative prompt templates. Use placeholders that are filled deterministically via a seeded shuffle.
- RNG control: loadgen must accept a deterministic seed parameter. Persist the seed used for every run in the run metadata.
- Sampling: set temperature/sampling flags to deterministic settings (temperature=0, top_k/top_p fixed) unless the metric under test requires stochastic sampling.

Priming strategies (practical recipes):
1) Cold-to-warm ramp (recommended for most throughput baselines):
   - Phase 0: node-level startup and model load (not measured).
   - Phase 1 (priming): inject Npriming requests (default 200–2000 depending on sequence length) at low concurrency to fill KV caches and warm kernels. Duration-based alternative: 2–5 minutes.
   - Phase 2 (ramp): ramp QPS/concurrency up to target over 30–120s to allow batching paths to stabilize.
   - Phase 3 (measure): run steady-state measurement window (10–30 minutes) capturing metrics.
2) Deterministic prefix priming: send a curated set of prefix requests (same content each run) to create identical KV states. Use for synthetic repeatability when distribution drift is not desired.
3) Randomized seeded priming: use a fixed RNG seed that selects priming prompts from the template corpus. Good balance between realism and reproducibility.
4) Anchor-based priming: insert 1–3 anchor requests with sentinel token patterns that are easy to detect in traces; useful for aligning traces across telemetry.

Warmup knobs and recommended defaults:
- Npriming: 500 requests for mixed-length workloads; raise for very long contexts.
- Ramp duration: 60s for small models (<=16k context), 120s for larger setups.
- Batch-size target: set client-side preferred batch size to expected production average; avoid forcing max batch occupancy during warmup.
- KV-cache warm fraction: target 70–90% occupancy before measurement. Verify with a KV-hit metric.

Repeatability controls (engineering checklist):
- Software: pin model artifact hash, runtime git commit, CUDA driver and docker image tag.
- Infrastructure: pin instance type, disable autoscaling, disable non-deterministic co-tenants (use dedicated instance if possible).
- OS: set CPU governor to performance, disable power-saving C-states if they introduce noise in the environment.
- Time: ensure NTP sync; record epoch timestamp at start of run.
- RNG: set and record seeds for loadgen and any sampling components; use same seed for reruns.
- Environment: set environment variables that affect determinism (e.g., TF_CUDNN_DETERMINISTIC if applicable).
- Background processes: quiesce backup jobs, cron, and monitoring collection that could skew disk or CPU.

Instrumentation and telemetry collection policy:
- Metrics to capture every 1s: requests/sec, tokens/sec, p50/p90/p99 latency, success/error counts, batch size histogram, queue lengths, KV cache hit ratio.
- Host metrics: GPU util, GPU memory usage, SM occupancy, PCIe bandwidth, CPU pct, network egress.
- Tracing: enable request traces for 1 in N requests (sample-rate 1%) to reduce overhead; ensure anchors in priming allow alignment.
- Profilers: use sampling profilers at the end of the run (nvprof/CUPTI, perf) rather than continuous tracing to limit noise. Snapshots: start-of-measure, mid-measure, end-of-measure.
- Persist raw events and metrics with run id and seed to object storage for offline analysis.

Analysis and comparison methodology:
- Windowing: discard the first 5% of the measurement window for tail-biased metrics (optional).
- Aggregates: report median, mean, p90, p95, p99 for latency; tokens/sec and requests/sec with 95% CI from repeated runs.
- Statistical checks: run at least 3 independent runs with different seeds for a given config to characterize variance. Use paired t-test or bootstrap to compare configs.
- Drift detection: flag a candidate regression if p99 latency increases by >10% and is significant (p<0.05) across runs.
- Attribution: correlate throughput drops with increases in batch wait time, kernel launch latencies, or GPU memory paging events.

Example loadgen snippet (pseudo-JSON, replace fields as needed):
{
  "seed": 15321,
  "arrival_pattern": "poisson",
  "target_qps": 1200,
  "ramp_seconds": 60,
  "priming_requests": 500,
  "sequence_distribution_file": "assets/seq-dist/2024-09-mix.json",
  "sampling": {
    "temperature": 0.0
  }
}

Operational playbook (run checklist):
- [ ] Pin model artifact and runtime commit; record hashes.
- [ ] Reserve dedicated instance(s) and snapshot instance config.
- [ ] Start metrics ingestion pipeline; verify end-to-end.
- [ ] Run Phase 0-3 as defined above; capture full run metadata.
- [ ] Upload traces and metrics; tag run id + seed in storage.
- [ ] Run automated analysis job and sanity checks; review heatmaps.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Noise from background cluster activity: isolate tests to a maintenance window or dedicated nodes.
- KV warmup mistaken for performance regression: always rerun with deterministic priming to validate.
- Over-aggressive warmup causing resource thrashing: prefer modest priming sized to reach ~80% KV occupancy.
- Long runs producing huge trace volumes: sample traces and rely on aggregates for the main dashboard.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How many priming requests are sufficient for very long-context runs (>=100k tokens)? (Action: run a priming-saturation sweep.)
- Can we automate detection of when a warmup succeeded (KV-hit plateauing) and gate measurement automatically?
- Should CI enforce a seeded-run policy for all regression checks?

Next steps:
- Implement a seeded-priming mode in bench-runner (GH PR linked above).
- Add a KV-occupancy metric export to the runtime and expose it in the console for run validation.
- Run a 10x priming sweep across our standard models and collect saturation curves.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we prioritize reproducibility in the most common throughput regimes rather than complete theoretical determinism.
- If you run these recipes and see unexpected variance, include the run id and seed when filing an issue so we can replay.

End of playbook.
